Subject: Denis, stop the sale and call me

Denis,

I am writing in English because I want this to be clear. I have tried to write this several times, and each time I get too angry to finish. I am still angry. But you are my brother, and I want you to understand what you have done and what I am asking you to do now.

On Thursday at six in the morning, I was in the bakery shaping baguettes when a photographer from the real estate agency walked into my shop. That is how I found out you were putting Papa’s building on the market. Not from you. From a stranger with a camera.

He told me you had said I was okay with it.

I had not agreed to this, Denis. I did not even know about it. I had to hear it standing in my own bakery, in the middle of my workday, with Karine having to calm me down. I am not proud of how upset I got, and I know the photographer was not the person responsible. But imagine for one minute being in my place.

Afterward, I went online and found the listing on Centris. $1,150,000. Papa’s building on rue Saint-Hubert, with my bakery downstairs and the two apartments above, advertised for sale while I knew nothing about it.

How did we get from “we decide together” to this?

You called me after Maman’s funeral and told me, “No rush, we decide together.” I remember those words very clearly. Maman died in February. The estate was settled in August. The building is now half yours and half mine. I believed that before either of us did anything this important, we would talk. Even if we disagreed, at least we would talk.

You live in Calgary, but I am here. I am the one who opens the bakery, who works in that building, who has to face the employees and the customers and wonder what happens next. That does not make your half less yours. But it makes it impossible for me to understand how you could take this step without calling me.

I also need you to stop treating this as if I am only being sentimental.

Of course I have feelings about the building. Papa bought it in 1979. Do you remember when we were children and he let you sleep in the room at the back where he kept the flour sacks? You loved being there. You have your own memories of that place. I know you do.

But I have also spent 31 years building a business there. Thirty-one years of early mornings, regular customers, difficult months, and work that still has to get done whether I am tired or worried or grieving. There are six employees whose jobs matter. There are customers who have been coming for years and who depend on finding us there. This is my living, Denis. At 57, I cannot treat the possibility of losing it as a small inconvenience.

I pay $2,400 a month in rent to the estate, and I have never been late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 of my own money for the new roof. I am not putting those numbers here to pretend they settle every question between us. I am putting them here because I want you to acknowledge that I have taken real financial responsibility for this place. I have not just been sitting downstairs enjoying the family building.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. That is not far away. I do not know what a buyer would do, and that uncertainty is frightening. If a developer buys it, will they want condos? Will they try to demolish it? Will I be faced with rent I cannot afford when my lease ends? I cannot survive my rent doubling. I cannot simply pack up 31 years of business and assume it will all work somewhere else.

And there was already another possibility on the table.

In September, I told you on the phone that I wanted to buy your half. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. That was a serious conversation for me. I had gone to the caisse because I wanted to find a way for you to receive money for your share without putting the bakery at risk.

I understand that $410,000 is not half of the asking price in the listing. I am not asking you to ignore that difference or pretending we have already agreed on a value. We need to discuss the value, the financing, and whether there is a way to make this work. But why did you not come back to me? If you thought my offer was too low, you could have said so. If you needed the money sooner, you could have told me. If something had changed, you could have picked up the phone.

Instead, I found out from the agency. It felt as though you had decided it was easier to let someone else face me. That hurt almost as much as the sale itself.

Here is what I am asking you to do.

Please have the building taken off the market this week so we can have a proper discussion. Tell the agent immediately that I did not agree to this and that nobody should be sent into the bakery again without arranging it with me in advance.

If you will not take it off the market, then at the very least give me the first opportunity to buy your half before you commit to a sale to someone else. I want a real opportunity, with the price and terms clearly laid out and reasonable time to speak with the caisse. Not a conversation after everything has already been decided.

I am willing to sit down with you and the appropriate professionals to work through the numbers. I am willing to hear what you need. I am not asking you to wait forever, and I am not saying that because I run the bakery, you have no say. I am asking for the same respect in return.

I need you to call me yourself, this week. Please do not answer this with a text from your wife. I am writing in English so there is no confusion, but this is a conversation you and I need to have directly. I want to hear your voice and understand what happened. I also need you to hear me, even if what I have to say is difficult.

I am furious with you. I will not pretend otherwise to make this email easier to read. You broke a promise I trusted, and you left me feeling that my work and my future were being discussed without me.

But I do not want to lose my brother over this. We have already lost Maman, and I do not want us to stop speaking or spend the rest of our lives with this between us. That is why I am writing instead of only shouting. I still want us to find a solution.

Please stop the sale, give us a chance to work this out, and call me.
